items.title: 5.7 Area of a Triangular Region Whose Vertices are Given

source_refs.note: Book p. 157-158: 5.7 Area of a Triangular Region, trapezium derivation (Figure 5.10), Note box, determinant formula, Corollary, Examples 14-15

blocks.text: To find the area of triangular region whose vertices are: \(P(x_1, y_1)\), \(Q(x_2, y_2)\) and \(R(x_3, y_3)\).

blocks.alt: Coordinate axes with origin O. A shaded triangle with vertices P(x1, y1) on the left, R(x3, y3) at the top and Q(x2, y2) on the right. Dashed perpendiculars PL, RM and QN drop to the x-axis, with heights y1, y3, y2. Below the axis, LM is marked x3 minus x1, MN is x2 minus x3, and LN is x2 minus x1.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.10: triangle PQR with perpendiculars PL, RM, QN to the x-axis (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text: Area of triangular region \(PQR\) = Area of trapezoidal region \(PLMR\) + Area of trapezoidal region \(RMNQ\) \(-\) Area of trapezoidal region \(PLNQ\)

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text:
A trapezium is a quadrilateral having two parallel and two non-parallel sides.
Area of trapezoidal region \(= \frac{1}{2}\)(sum of \(\parallel\) sides)(distance between \(\parallel\) sides).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why trapeziums? Each of \(PLMR\), \(RMNQ\), \(PLNQ\) has two vertical sides (the perpendiculars), which are parallel. Their lengths are just the \(y\)-coordinates, and the distance between them is measured along the \(x\)-axis, the difference of the \(x\)-coordinates.
Look at Figure 5.10: the two upper trapeziums together cover the triangle plus the trapezium \(PLNQ\) under it. Taking \(PLNQ\) away leaves exactly the triangle.
In the figure the points lie above the \(x\)-axis and \(x_1 < x_3 < x_2\); the final formula is true for any position of the points.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How the lines follow: \(|\overline{PL}| = y_1\), \(|\overline{RM}| = y_3\), \(|\overline{QN}| = y_2\), and \(|\overline{LM}| = x_3 - x_1\), \(|\overline{MN}| = x_2 - x_3\), \(|\overline{LN}| = x_2 - x_1\).
After multiplying out, \(x_3y_3\), \(x_1y_1\) and \(x_2y_2\) each appear once with \(+\) and once with \(-\), so they cancel. Six terms remain.
Thus, the required area is given by:

blocks.text_alt: Delta equals one half of: x1 times (y2 minus y3), plus x2 times (y3 minus y1), plus x3 times (y1 minus y2)

blocks.latex: \Delta = \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{vmatrix} x_1 & y_1 & 1 \\ x_2 & y_2 & 1 \\ x_3 & y_3 & 1 \end{vmatrix}
blocks.text_alt: Delta equals one half of the determinant with rows x1 y1 1, x2 y2 1, x3 y3 1

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why does the determinant give the same thing? Expand it along the third column (all 1s): \(1(x_2y_3 - x_3y_2) - 1(x_1y_3 - x_3y_1) + 1(x_1y_2 - x_2y_1)\). These are exactly the six terms of the line above.
Sign: the formula is positive when \(P \to Q \to R\) goes anticlockwise (as in Figure 5.10) and negative when it goes clockwise. Area is never negative, so if you get a negative number, take its absolute value.
If the points \(P\), \(Q\) and \(R\) are collinear, then \(\Delta = 0\)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Three points on one line enclose no region, so the area is zero. The converse is also true: if \(\Delta = 0\) the points are collinear. This gives a quick test for collinearity, used in Example 15.

blocks.title: Example 14
blocks.problem: Find the area of the region bounded by the triangle with vertices \(A(a, b)\), \(B(-a, b)\) and \(C(0, -b)\).
steps:
Given: \(A(a, b)\), \(B(-a, b)\), \(C(0, -b)\).
To find: the area \(\Delta\) of triangle \(ABC\).
Method: the determinant formula \(\Delta = \frac{1}{2}\begin{vmatrix} x_1 & y_1 & 1 \\ x_2 & y_2 & 1 \\ x_3 & y_3 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\): each row is one vertex followed by 1.

Step 1: write the determinant
\[\Delta = \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{vmatrix} a & b & 1 \\ -a & b & 1 \\ 0 & -b & 1 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: rows are \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) in order.

Step 2: expand along the first row
\[= \tfrac{1}{2}\big[a(b + b) - b(-a - 0)\]
\[+ 1(ab - 0)\big]\]
Why: the signs along a row are \(+, -, +\). The minor of \(a\) is \(b \cdot 1 - 1 \cdot (-b) = b + b\); of \(b\) is \(-a \cdot 1 - 1 \cdot 0 = -a\); of 1 is \((-a)(-b) - b \cdot 0 = ab\).

Check:
\(A\) and \(B\) are on the line \(y = b\), so the base \(AB = 2a\). The height is the distance of \(C(0, -b)\) from \(y = b\), which is \(2b\).
\[\tfrac{1}{2} \times 2a \times 2b = 2ab \;\checkmark\]
(For \(a, b > 0\). In general the area is \(|2ab|\).)
blocks.answer: The area of \(\Delta ABC\) is \(2ab\) square units.

blocks.title: Example 15
blocks.problem: Find the area of the region bounded by the triangle with vertices \(A(1, 2)\), \(B(3, 6)\) and \(C(5, 10)\).
steps:
Given: \(A(1, 2)\), \(B(3, 6)\), \(C(5, 10)\).
To find: the area \(\Delta\) of the region bounded by triangle \(ABC\).
Method: the determinant formula. First make zeros with row operations so that the expansion is short.

Step 1: write the determinant and subtract \(R_1\)
\[\Delta = \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 6 & 1 \\ 5 & 10 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0 \end{vmatrix}\]
by \(R_2 - R_1\) and \(R_3 - R_1\).
Why: subtracting one row from another does not change a determinant, and it turns the 1s in the third column into 0s.

Step 2: expand by the 3rd column
\[= \tfrac{1}{2}\left[1\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 4 & 8 \end{vmatrix}\right]\]
\[= \tfrac{1}{2}[16 - 16] = 0\]
Why: only the top entry of the third column is non-zero; its sign is \(+\) and its minor is \(2 \cdot 8 - 4 \cdot 4\).

Step 3: conclusion
The 'triangle' has zero area, so it is not a real triangle: the given points are collinear.
Why: Corollary of 5.7: \(\Delta = 0\) exactly when the three points lie on one line.

Check:
\[m_{AB} = \dfrac{6 - 2}{3 - 1} = 2\]
\[m_{BC} = \dfrac{10 - 6}{5 - 3} = 2\]
Equal slopes through the common point \(B\), so \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) are on one line \(\checkmark\).
blocks.answer: \(\Delta = 0\); thus, the given points are collinear.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\Delta = \frac{1}{2}[x_1(y_2 - y_3) + x_2(y_3 - y_1) + x_3(y_1 - y_2)]\), or the determinant with rows \((x_i, y_i, 1)\) times \(\frac{1}{2}\).
2. It comes from three trapeziums: two added, one subtracted.
3. A negative value means the vertices were taken clockwise; the area is the absolute value.
4. \(\Delta = 0\) if and only if the three points are collinear.
5. Row operations (like \(R_2 - R_1\)) make zeros and shorten the expansion.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Forgetting the factor \(\frac{1}{2}\).
2. Giving a negative area; always report \(|\Delta|\).
3. Wrong sign pattern in the expansion: along a row or column it is \(+, -, +\).
4. Mixing up the order inside \(x_1(y_2 - y_3) + x_2(y_3 - y_1) + x_3(y_1 - y_2)\): the indices go round in a cycle 1, 2, 3.
